executive_summary.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology commissioned a secure source code review of KavachBank. The review was performed on 12 November 2026 with CodeKavach, combining deterministic rule and taint analysis with model-assisted triage under a privacy-preserving egress policy. 30 files and 947 lines of YAML, Python, Unknown, JavaScript, Dockerfile, Terraform code were analysed.

The review identified 59 findings (15 critical, 27 high, 12 medium, 5 low). The overall security posture is rated critical: at least one weakness can be exploited to compromise the application or its data, and immediate action is required. 6 findings are supported by a complete source-to-sink data-flow trace.

executive_summary.heading: Most significant findings
bullets: CK-2026-001 (Critical): A pull_request_target workflow checks out the pull request head, running untrusted code with repository secrets and a write token. An attacker can run code with the pipeline's secrets and write token, tamper with releases and pivot into the supply chain.
CK-2026-002 (Critical): Container 'api' is privileged. Any other weakness in the component becomes a full host or cluster compromise, because the attacker inherits the excess privileges.

CK-2026-003 (Critical): Data from a http_param source reaches a sql sink (cur.execute). If account_id is attacker-controlled, an attacker could alter the query predicate and potentially retrieve unauthorized database rows; broader effects depend on the database driver and permissions.

CK-2026-004 (Critical): Hard-coded credential of type connection_string (masked preview po****** (51 chars), entropy 4.91 bits/char). Anyone with access to the repository, a build artefact or a decompiled binary obtains the credential; rotating it requires a code change and redeployment.

CK-2026-005 (Critical): Hard-coded credential of type aws_access_key (masked preview AK****** (20 chars), entropy 3.68 bits/char). Anyone with access to the repository, a build artefact or a decompiled binary obtains the credential; rotating it requires a code change and redeployment.

executive_summary.heading: Where the weaknesses concentrate
paragraphs: The most frequent weakness classes are CWE-798 Use of Hard-coded Credentials (11); CWE-250 Execution with Unnecessary Privileges (8); CWE-1395 Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component (8). By OWASP Top 10 category the largest group is A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures (12 findings). Recurring classes indicate a missing shared control rather than isolated mistakes, so the recommendations below address the control as well as each instance.

executive_summary.heading: Strategic recommendations
bullets: Immediate (within 7 days): Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately, then load it at run time from a secret manager or environment. [CK-2026-004, CK-2026-005, CK-2026-006, CK-2026-007 and others]
Immediate (within 7 days): Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed. [CK-2026-015]
Short term (within 30 days): Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed. [CK-2026-026, CK-2026-027, CK-2026-038, CK-2026-040 and others]
Short term (within 30 days): Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs. [CK-2026-018, CK-2026-019, CK-2026-021, CK-2026-022]
Medium term (within 90 days): Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs. [CK-2026-043, CK-2026-044, CK-2026-047]
Medium term (within 90 days): Encode output for its HTML context (or use a template engine with auto-escaping) and never send raw request data with res.send or equivalent. [CK-2026-051, CK-2026-054]
Planned (next release cycle): Do not check out untrusted code in privileged workflows; pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and reduce the token permissions. [CK-2026-058, CK-2026-059]
Planned (next release cycle): Pin the component to a reviewed version or digest and replace unmaintained components. [CK-2026-055, CK-2026-057]
Embed the deterministic rules in CI so that the weakness classes found here are blocked at pull-request time, and schedule a retest once the fixes are deployed.

roadmap.action: Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately, then load it at run time from a secret manager or environment.
Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed.
Use a safe loader (for example yaml.safe_load or JSON) that builds plain data only; never unpickle data from an untrusted source.
Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs.

roadmap.theme: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
roadmap.action: Do not check out untrusted code in privileged workflows; pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and reduce the token permissions.
Stop passing the command to a shell: call the program with an argument list (shell=False) and validate each argument against a strict allow-list.
Use parameterised queries or prepared statements for every value that reaches the query; never format user data into SQL text.
Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed.
Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs.
Scope every lookup to the authenticated principal (for example WHERE owner_id = current_user) and return 404 for records the caller does not own.
Resolve the final path and reject it unless it lies inside an allow-listed base directory; prefer opaque identifiers mapped server-side to file names.
Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately, then load it at run time from a secret manager or environment.

roadmap.theme: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere
roadmap.action: Restrict the exposure to the intended network or principals.
Re-enable certificate and hostname verification.
Use at least 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit elliptic curves and AES-128 or stronger.

roadmap.theme: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource
roadmap.action: Tighten the permissions to the owning principal only.
Add the authentication and authorisation guard used elsewhere in the service to this route, defaulting to deny.
Stop passing the command to a shell: call the program with an argument list (shell=False) and validate each argument against a strict allow-list.
Generate a fresh random IV (or nonce) for every encryption with a CSPRNG and store it alongside the ciphertext.
Add the missing access check, denying by default.
Validate the destination against an allow-list of hosts and schemes and block private, loopback and link-local address ranges after DNS resolution.

roadmap.theme: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
roadmap.action: Hash passwords with a slow, salted, memory-hard function such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, and migrate existing hashes on next login.
Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs.
Encode output for its HTML context (or use a template engine with auto-escaping) and never send raw request data with res.send or equivalent.

roadmap.theme: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
roadmap.action: Verify a pinned checksum or signature before executing downloaded artefacts.
Disable debug mode and remove debug endpoints from production builds.
Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed.

roadmap.theme: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere
roadmap.action: Restrict the exposure to the intended network or principals.
Restrict allowed origins to a known list.
Encrypt the data in transit with TLS and at rest with a managed key.

roadmap.theme: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
roadmap.action: Do not check out untrusted code in privileged workflows; pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and reduce the token permissions.

findings.likelihood_rationale: OWASP likelihood high; confirmed source-to-sink path

lines.text: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM premium_accounts WHERE id = '%s'" % account_id)

verdict.reasoning: Line 6 inserts account_id directly into a SQL statement using Python string formatting before passing it to cur.execute; this is string construction, not database parameter binding. The data path from account_id to the potential SQL sink is direct and satisfiable, and no escaping, validation, or sink-appropriate sanitizer appears. However, the excerpt does not establish that account_id can be influenced by an attacker, so exploitability cannot be confirmed without a caller of find_premium_account.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a sql sink (cur.execute). A database query is built by concatenating or interpolating data that an external party controls, so that data is parsed as SQL rather than treated as a value.
findings.impact: If account_id is attacker-controlled, an attacker could alter the query predicate and potentially retrieve unauthorized database rows; broader effects depend on the database driver and permissions.
findings.remediation_short_term: If account_id is attacker-influenced, pass it separately using the database driver's parameterized-query API and its required placeholder syntax rather than formatting it into the SQL string.
findings.remediation_long_term: Standardise on an ORM or query builder that parameterises by default, restrict the database account to the least privilege required, and add query-construction checks to code review and CI.
references: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

findings.description: Hard-coded credential of type razorpay_key_id (masked preview rz****** (23 chars), entropy 4.26 bits/char). A credential such as a password, API key or token is embedded in the source code.
findings.impact:
An attacker can impersonate the application to Razorpay and exercise all API capabilities granted to this credential pair. Depending on account scope, this may expose payment and customer metadata and permit transaction-affecting operations, potentially causing unauthorized refunds, financial loss, or corrupted payment state.

Attack scenario: An attacker obtains read access to a source repository, deployment image, backup, or server artifact containing `services/web/config.js`. They extract `razorpayKeyId` and `razorpayKeySecret`, authenticate to the Razorpay API, and use the credentials to retrieve payment-related records or perform permitted state-changing actions, such as issuing refunds, until the credentials are revoked.

Affected: Razorpay merchant account and API-authorized operations; Payment, order, and customer metadata accessible through the credentials; Financial and transaction integrity where the credentials permit refunds or other state-changing operations

Preconditions: The attacker must be able to read the source or a deployment artifact containing the literals. The credential pair must still be valid, and meaningful financial impact requires live-environment credentials with permission for transaction-affecting API operations. If the credentials are test-only, expired, or revoked, the practical impact is substantially lower.
findings.remediation_short_term:
1. Revoke and rotate the exposed `razorpayKeyId`/`razorpayKeySecret` credential pair immediately.
2. Store the replacements in a managed secrets service, or inject them as protected deployment environment variables.
3. Replace both literals with runtime lookups and do not provide hard-coded fallback values.
4. Validate at startup that both values are present and terminate without printing them if either is missing.
5. Remove the credentials from repository history, build artifacts, caches, and deployment bundles, then redeploy using the rotated values.
6. Ensure local secret files are excluded from version control and are not copied into container images.

Secure example:
```javascript
razorpayKeyId: process.env.razorpayKeyId,
  razorpayKeySecret: process.env.razorpayKeySecret,
```

Defence in depth:
- Enable repository and CI secret scanning with push protection for future commits.
- Restrict secret-store access to the application identity, use separate credentials per environment, and grant only required permissions.
- Prevent configuration and environment values from appearing in logs, diagnostics, error reports, or support bundles.
findings.remediation_long_term: Adopt a secret manager, add pre-commit and CI secret scanning, and purge the value from version-control history.
references: OWASP Top 10 2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a path sink (fs.createReadStream). A file-system path is built from data an external party controls without checking that the resolved path stays inside the intended directory.
findings.impact:
An attacker can select and read files outside the intended directory, up to the permissions of the server process. This can disclose application secrets, configuration, source code, private data, or credentials that enable further compromise. The shown code does not provide file modification or code execution directly.

Attack scenario: An attacker requests the affected endpoint with `req.query.file` set to a traversal path such as `../../../../path/to/a/sensitive/file`, potentially URL-encoded. After query decoding, `path.join` resolves the path outside the intended directory, and `fs.createReadStream` reads the selected file. If `pipe(res)` returns the stream through the response, the attacker receives its contents.

Affected: Files readable by the server process outside the directory identified by `config.exportDir`; Application source code, configuration, credentials, tokens, or other sensitive local data; Accounts or external services whose credentials are stored in readable files

Preconditions: The HTTP handler must be reachable, the attacker must control `req.query.file`, traversal components must survive request parsing, and the target file must be readable by the server process. Actual remote disclosure also depends on `pipe(res)` exposing the created stream to the requester; its behavior is not shown.
findings.remediation_short_term: Resolve the candidate against a canonical base directory and reject it unless path.relative confirms it remains beneath that base. Prefer an allowlist of permitted filenames, and account for symlink escapes when untrusted users can affect filesystem entries.
findings.remediation_long_term: Centralise file access behind a storage service that enforces containment, and run the process with a file-system view restricted to the data it needs.
references: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

If it is freshly generated using a cryptographically secure source for every call, the finding is false. verdict.reasoning: The sink at line 14 is security-relevant because req.query.file influences the file opened by fs.createReadStream. However, path.resolve at line 9 normalizes absolute paths and parent-directory components, and the check at line 10 permits the sink only when the resulting path begins with the resolved base directory plus path.sep. The separator prevents sibling-prefix bypasses, while rejected paths return at line 12. Thus ordinary absolute-path and `..` traversal cannot reach the sink. This does not address pre-existing symbolic links inside root, but the shown request input cannot create such links and there is no evidence that an attacker controls the filesystem namespace.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a path sink (fs.createReadStream). A file-system path is built from data an external party controls without checking that the resolved path stays inside the intended directory.
findings.impact: An attacker can read or overwrite files outside the intended directory, including configuration files, credentials and other customers' documents.
findings.remediation_short_term: Do not use request data as a file path. Map user input to an identifier in an allow-list, or resolve the joined path (os.path.realpath / Path.resolve) and reject it unless it stays inside the intended base directory; use werkzeug.utils.safe_join or an equivalent helper.
findings.remediation_long_term: Centralise file access behind a storage service that enforces containment, and run the process with a file-system view restricted to the data it needs.
references: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

findings.likelihood_rationale: OWASP likelihood high; entry point network; confirmed source-to-sink path

verdict.reasoning: The sink is security-relevant because res.send constructs an HTML response. Attacker-controlled req.query.name is concatenated directly into an HTML text context. The path is unconditional and therefore satisfiable. No validation, contextual output encoding, or other effective sanitizer appears before the sink, so a value containing closing tags and executable markup can alter the response DOM.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a html sink (res.send). Data from the request is written into an HTML response without context-aware output encoding, so a browser may interpret it as markup or script.
findings.impact:
An attacker can execute JavaScript in another user's browser in the application's security origin. This permits page modification and phishing, access to non-HttpOnly origin data, and authenticated actions using the victim's session. The exact account and data impact depends on the functionality available on that origin.

Attack scenario: An attacker creates a URL to `renderGreeting`'s route with an HTML/JavaScript payload in the `name` query parameter and convinces a signed-in user to open it. The server reflects the payload through `res.send`; the victim's browser renders the response and executes the injected script under the application's origin. The script can read origin-accessible data or issue authenticated requests as the victim.

Affected: Users' browser sessions and any application data accessible to client-side code on the same origin; Integrity of the rendered page and actions performed through the victim's account

Preconditions: The route must be reachable with an attacker-supplied `name` query parameter, the response must be interpreted as HTML, and a victim must open the crafted URL. Effective protections such as a restrictive Content Security Policy must not prevent the chosen payload. Account compromise or data access additionally depends on what authenticated functionality and browser-accessible data exist on the same origin.
findings.remediation_short_term:
1. Add a maintained HTML-encoding library such as `escape-html` as a direct dependency.
2. Convert `req.query.name` to a string and encode it immediately before insertion into the HTML text context.
3. Keep encoding context-specific; use the appropriate encoder if the value is later placed in an attribute, URL, CSS, or JavaScript context.
4. Prefer an auto-escaping template engine for larger HTML responses.

Secure example:
```javascript
res.send(
  '<xx>xxxxxxx xxxx, ' +
  require('escape-html')(String(req.query.name ?? '')) +
  '</xx>'
);
```

Defence in depth:
- Apply a restrictive Content-Security-Policy that disallows inline scripts.
- Validate the field's type, length, and expected business format before rendering it; validation does not replace output encoding.
- Add regression tests with HTML metacharacters and executable-markup payloads to verify they are displayed only as text.
findings.remediation_long_term: Adopt auto-escaping templates throughout, deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy, and set HttpOnly on session cookies.
references: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

findings.remediation_short_term: Bind request data only to an explicit allow-list of fields (DTOs), never merge untrusted objects into prototypes or configuration, and load code and libraries only from fixed, trusted locations.
findings.remediation_long_term: Separate untrusted builds from privileged jobs and review CI configuration as code.

privacy_attestation.not_covered: What this attestation does not cover. The zero-leak check is verbatim: it looks for the listed terms as written and does not detect a term that was paraphrased, split or encoded. The structure of the code, its control flow, the libraries it uses and the technology stack are still disclosed to the model whatever the privacy level. Structural leakage, meaning what an observer could infer from that structure, is measured separately by the evaluation harness and is not part of this check.
